unit_label: CB Module E unit 2: development, regulation and supervision and recent performance of scheduled commercial banks (courseware unit 14)

facts.statement: Development of commercial banks 1950-1991 (courseware): the banking system in India has witnessed steady growth since independence; the inadequacy of the banking system in terms of its number and size as well as in the supply of financial products in line with economic development was realised since the beginning of the planning process in the 1950s; financial institutions came into existence to meet the diverse requirements of a growing economy both short-term and long-term financing requirements. Nationalisation of banks in 1969 was an important step in steering the banking system to achieve social goals of socialistic pattern of society, particularly meeting the financial needs of agriculture, industry and trade and commerce. The financial sector reforms ushered in the 1990s were another milestone in bank sector development; efficiency in the allocation of credit improved after liberalisation, private investments have grown and financial deepening increased; financial liberalisation has generally resulted in more effective monetary policy. Initial years (1950 to 1969): before 1950 there were several bank failures; the supervisory powers conferred initially in 1940 vested the Reserve Bank with the right, on a restricted scale, to inspect banking companies in consultation with the Government; the Banking Companies (Inspection) Ordinance, 1946 gave the Reserve Bank more specific powers to inspect banking companies without the prior consent of the banking company; under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 the Reserve Bank is required to satisfy itself by inspecting the books of accounts and methods of operation of the banking company, before granting a licence, that the company is in a position to pay its depositors in full as their claims accrue; the purpose of the inspections shifted from a quantitative assessment of the real or exchangeable value of the paid-up capital and reserves to a qualitative appraisal of its financial position, management and methods of operation; in July 1949 the policy of instituting systematic periodical inspections of all banking companies was announced; in February 1950 it was decided that all banking companies would be inspected in turn, irrespective of their size and standing, and that such inspections would be a regular feature of the Reserve Bank supervisory activities. The focus of regulation and supervision during the 1950s was to facilitate the creation of a structure of banking sector to cater to the requirements of the nascent economy; the Reserve Bank commenced systematic periodical inspections of all banks in March 1950. The Banking Regulation Act, 1949 brought certain loopholes in the law in dealing with managerial irregularities; the Act was amended in January 1957, with provisions such as enabling clauses to offer refinance facilities to banks, and enactment of the SBI Act. The collapse of the Palai Central Bank and Laxmi Commercial Bank in 1960 impacted several aspects of the Reserve Bank policy towards commercial banks; the Reserve Bank acquired new powers to predicate amalgamations and the speedier de-licensing; in 1961 the Reserve Bank reorganised and strengthened its inspection function; the Reserve Bank evinced keen interest in evolving capital adequacy norms as well as introducing a deposit insurance scheme; between 1960 and 1968 the thrust of the regulatory and supervisory function was on ensuring soundness of operations of banks and consolidation and protection of the interests of the small depositors through various measures including compulsory amalgamations and liquidations; the deposit insurance scheme was also introduced during this period; through the branch licensing policy the Reserve Bank started correcting the lopsided branch distribution of Indian banking; the concept of social control was recognised in 1967 over issues related to deployment of credit. Nationalisation and consolidation (1969-1991): the nationalisation of 14 major commercial banks on July 19, 1969 was a turning point; the focus of regulation was therefore appropriately re-oriented to meet the objectives of the nationalisation of banks; the Central Government in consultation with the Reserve Bank constituted the first Board of Directors for each of the nationalised banks on July 18, 1970; the National Credit Council (NCC) suggested certain revisions in the branch licensing policy; the Lead Bank Scheme was introduced in December 1969; in 1972 the Reserve Bank conceived a perspective plan calling for a branch expansion programme covering three years, 1972 to 1974; to strengthen the supervisory mechanism further, it was decided to institute a new type of inspection during 1977-78, viz., Annual Appraisal of banks in addition to the Financial Appraisal; during the 1980s the Reserve Bank regulatory and supervisory function focused on priority sector lending: in 1980 it was decided that public sector banks would aim at raising the proportion of their advances to priority sectors to 40 per cent by 1985; in 1980 six more banks were nationalised; with effect from January 1985 a system of Annual Financial Review was introduced to be conducted after the annual audit of the bank branches; the Reserve Bank appointed a Working Group in December 1981 to review the system of inspection of commercial banks in the public and the private sectors; in the middle of the 1980s the system entered its phase of consolidation, diversification and liberalisation. Reforms of the 1990s: the decade of the 1990s was a watershed; notwithstanding the remarkable progress made in achieving social goals during the 1980s, it experienced certain problems that led to decline in efficiency and productivity and erosion of profitability; the Committee on the Financial System (Chairman: M. Narasimham, 1991) was constituted; the RBI initiated several measures such as deregulation of interest rates, reduction of statutory pre-emptions such as CRR and SLR, and provision of operational autonomy to banks; various prudential measures that conformed to the global best practices were also implemented; following the Narasimham Committee recommendations, guidelines to facilitate entry of the private sector banks were issued in 1993 to foster greater competition and achieving higher productivity and efficiency of the banking system.

Prudential requirements, returns and risk management (courseware): most central banks have adopted the Basle principles of bank supervision while specifying the prudential requirements; the areas where emphasis is laid are the capital adequacy norms, asset classification procedures and methods, income recognition principles, market valuation of assets and recovery mechanisms to reduce the non-performing assets of banks; central banks in EMEs often tend to rely on both on-site and off-site supervision; the micro-prudential indicators reflect the inherent strength of each bank and when aggregated give the aggregate micro-prudential indicator (AMPI) for the banking system as a whole; the categories: capital adequacy (capital ratio), asset quality (sectoral credit concentration, foreign currency lending, non-performing loans and provisions, loans to loss-making public sector entities, connected lending), management soundness (expense ratios, earnings per employee), earnings and profitability (return on assets, return on equity, income and expense ratios), liquidity (central bank credit to financial institutions, deposits in relation to monetary aggregates, segmentation of inter-bank rates, loans to deposit ratios), systems and controls (procedures for risk management, audit compliance and internal inspection), sensitivity to market risk (foreign exchange, interest rate, equity price and commodity price risk) and market-based indicators; the acronym CAMELS; stress tests; macroeconomic indicators (MEIs) and the macro-prudential indicators (MPIs); the AMPIs and MPIs are linked to arrive at what may be called the macro-prudential indicators; the European Central Bank and the Bank of England take note. Returns: the Reserve Bank issued the ALM guidelines in 1999 which, inter alia, introduced two returns viz. Statements of Structural Liquidity and Interest Rate Sensitivity in domestic currency covering domestic operations; in November 2012 the RBI revised the liquidity risk management guidelines to align with the new standards and monitoring tools issued by the BCBS in September 2008 and December 2010; the revised guidelines also introduced two additional returns viz., liquidity coverage ratio (LCR) and net stable funding ratio (NSFR) as set out in the Basel III liquidity standards; as regards management of interest rate risk, the 1999 ALM guidelines prescribed the earnings perspective using the Traditional Gap Analysis (TGA); in November 2012 revised guidelines were issued which advised banks to manage the interest rate risk using the duration gap analysis (DGA) in addition to the existing TGA; returns: Statement of Structural Liquidity (fortnightly): Part A1 domestic currency Indian operations, A2 foreign currency Indian operations, A3 combined Indian operations, Part B overseas operations, Part C consolidated bank operations; Basel III liquidity returns: LCR (BLR 1 monthly), funding concentration (BLR 2 monthly), unencumbered assets (BLR 3 quarterly), LCR by significant currency (BLR 4 monthly), other information on liquidity (BLR 5 monthly); interest rate risk (monthly): Statement of Traditional Gap Analysis (TGA) and Statement of Modified Duration Gap (interest rate sensitivity) for each currency. Risk management in banks (Box 14.1): banks face mainly four types of risks: market risk, credit risk, legal risk and operational risk; there is also systemic risk; the Reserve Bank issued guidelines on Risk Management Systems in Banks in October 1999 together with the ALM guidelines issued in February 1999 as a benchmark for banks to establish an integrated risk management system; salient features: organisational structure; comprehensive risk measurement approach; risk management policies approved by the Board; guidelines and parameters used to govern risk taking; MIS for reporting, monitoring and controlling risks; well-laid out procedures, effective internal control, and comprehensive risk reporting framework; risk management framework independent of operational departments; periodic review and evaluation; the primary responsibility of laying down risk parameters and establishing the risk management and control system has been vested with the Board of Directors; banks have been advised that the implementation of the integrated risk management system could be assigned to a Risk Management Committee or a Committee of Top Executives that reports to the Board; banks have also been advised to constitute a high-level Credit Policy Committee (CPC) to deal with issues relating to credit sanction, disbursement and follow-up procedures and to manage and control credit risk on a whole bank basis; banks have also been advised to concurrently set up an independent Credit Risk Management Department; the activities of Asset-Liability Management Committee (ALCO) and CPC for management of credit and market risks need to be integrated. Credit risk: the Loan Policy approved by the Board; a clearly defined scheme of delegation of powers; prudential norms on benchmark financial ratios, single borrower or borrower group exposure, substantial exposure, industry-specific, region-specific and sector-specific exposures; a comprehensive risk rating system; loan review mechanism for large value accounts; off-balance sheet exposures subject to rigorous evaluation; inter-bank exposure and country risk framework. Market risk: banks advised to adopt techniques like duration, earnings at risk (EaR), value at risk (VaR) and simulation; most large banks adopted Risk Adjusted Return on Capital (RAROC). Liquidity risk: measure on an ongoing basis. Interest rate risk: the gap analysis (RSL and RSA); gap limits with the approval of the Board; VaR, Duration and Simulation approaches; stress tests; Funds Transfer Pricing (FTP) mechanism; Net Interest Income (NII) and Economic Value or Market Value of Equity (MVE). Currency risk: banks are free to set gap limits with the approval of the Reserve Bank; value at risk approach for forward exposures; open position limits together with gap limits. Operational risk: banks advised to develop and adopt proper systems for measurement, monitoring and control of operational risk. Regulatory approaches to market risk: (a) building block approach (BBA), (b) the internal model approach (IMA), (c) the pre-commitment approach (PCA); the Basle Accord market risk capital standards (1988) represent an example of BBA.

Regulatory policies and supervision of scheduled commercial banks (courseware, 2020-22): Resolution Framework for Covid-19 stressed assets (announced 6 August 2020) allowed implementation of a resolution plan (RP) for eligible corporate exposures without change in ownership, and for personal loans, while classifying them as standard subject to certain conditions; borrowers classified as standard and not in default for more than 30 days with any lending institution as on March 1, 2020 and continued to be classified as standard till the date of invocation were eligible; the Expert Committee (Chairman: Shri K. V. Kamath) recommended five financial parameters for lending institutions (total outside liability/adjusted tangible net worth; total debt/EBITDA; current ratio; debt service coverage ratio; average debt service coverage ratio) and sector-specific thresholds; the resolution framework had to be invoked till December 31, 2020 with implementation within 90 days for personal loans and 180 days for other eligible loans from the date of invocation; Resolution Framework 2.0 (5 May 2021) for individuals and small businesses (aggregate exposure limit of Rs 50 crore as on March 31, 2021, invoked till 30 September 2021 with implementation in 90 days). Ex-gratia payment of difference between compound interest and simple interest: from October 23, 2020 scheme for borrowers with aggregate borrowing of up to Rs 2 crore for the moratorium period, March 1, 2020 to August 31, 2020. Loan-to-value ratio against gold ornaments: on August 6, 2020 the LTV for gold loans for non-agricultural end-uses was increased from 75 per cent to 90 per cent, applicable till March 31, 2021. Dividend declaration by banks: RBI directed banks not to make any dividend payment on equity shares from profits pertaining to 2019-20, to bolster provisions and conserve capital; reviewed for 2020-21. CRR: reduced to 3 per cent of NDTL effective March 28, 2020, restored to 3.5 per cent and 4 per cent in 2021 (March 27, 2021 and May 22, 2021). Credit to MSME entrepreneurs: from 5 February 2021 banks could deduct the amount equivalent to credit disbursed to new MSME borrowers up to Rs 25 lakh per borrower from their NDTL for CRR (till 1 October 2021, extended to 31 December 2021). HTM: banks were permitted to exceed the HTM ceiling up to an overall limit of 22 per cent (instead of 19.5 per cent) till March 31, 2023; the enhanced HTM limit to be restored to 19.5 per cent in phased manner. MSF: banks allowed to dip into SLR up to an additional one per cent of NDTL, cumulatively up to three per cent of NDTL, to meet LCR requirements (up to 31 December 2021; normal dispensation of two per cent restored from January 1, 2022). Deferment of last tranche of capital conservation buffer (CCB): the last tranche of 0.625 per cent was deferred to October 1, 2021 (and it has come into effect since then); NSFR implementation deferred to October 1, 2021. Regulatory retail portfolio (risk weight 75 per cent): exposure limit raised from Rs 5 crore to Rs 7.5 crore per counterparty to expand credit flow to small businesses. Rationalisation of risk weights for individual housing loans: for new individual housing loans sanctioned between October 16, 2020 and March 31, 2022, irrespective of the amount, risk weights linked to LTV ratio. Streamlining of opening of current accounts: from August 6, 2021 restrictions on opening and operating current accounts and CC/OD facilities for borrowers. Supervision of scheduled commercial banks: calibrated supervisory approach; Board for Financial Supervision (BFS, constituted in November 1994) acts as the integrated supervisor for the financial system covering SCBs, AIFIs, Co-operative banks and NBFCs; during July 2020 to November 2021, 16 meetings of the BFS; appointment of Statutory Central Auditors (SCAs) / Statutory Auditors (SAs) of SCBs (excluding RRBs), UCBs and NBFCs (including HFCs): guidelines issued in April 2021 (first time when such guidelines were prescribed for UCBs and NBFCs); objective: ensure independence of auditors, avoid conflict of interest in auditors appointments, improve the quality and standards of audit; responsibilities on the Board/Audit Committee of the Board. Revised Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) framework for SCBs effective January 1, 2022 (in contrast to the earlier framework, a negative return on assets (RoA) will no longer be a trigger to initiate PCA); Lakshmi Vilas Bank, which was under PCA, was amalgamated with DBS Bank on November 27, 2020; IDBI Bank and UCO Bank were taken out of PCA on March 10, 2021 and September 8, 2021; Indian Overseas Bank on September 29, 2021; only Central Bank of India remained under PCA. PCA framework: objective is to enable timely supervisory intervention at appropriate time and require the Supervised Entity to initiate and implement remedial measures in a timely manner, so as to restore its financial health; also a tool for market discipline; the PCA framework does not preclude RBI from taking any other action; for SCBs: Capital, Asset Quality and Leverage are the key areas for monitoring; indicators: CRAR/Common Equity Tier I ratio, Net NPA ratio and Tier I Leverage Ratio; breach of any risk threshold may result in invocation of PCA; applies to banks operating in India including foreign banks operating through branches or subsidiaries; a bank will generally be placed under PCA based on the Audited Annual Financial Results and the ongoing Supervisory Assessment; exit from PCA: if no breaches in risk thresholds in any of the parameters over four continuous quarterly financial statements, one of which should be Audited Annual Financial Statement, and based on supervisory comfort including an assessment on sustainability of profitability; restrictions (corrective actions): mandatory actions: restriction on dividend distribution/remittance of profits and promoters/owners/parent (for foreign banks) to bring in capital; restriction on branch expansion, domestic and/or overseas; appropriate restrictions on capital expenditure, other than technological upgradation within Board approved limits. Mergers of PSBs: in August 2019 the Government announced a mega-merger of 10 public sector banks into four; the anchor banks and the banks merged with them: PNB (Oriental Bank of Commerce and United Bank of India), Canara Bank (Syndicate Bank), Union Bank of India (Corporation Bank and Andhra Bank), Indian Bank (Allahabad Bank); from 1 April 2020 the customers of the merged bank are treated as customers of the anchor bank; merits of mergers: higher capital base, larger pool of money, scale of operations and efficiency, a wider customer base, more products, and banks better equipped to face global competition; to help banks manage associated risks, state-run banks to appoint specialised Chief Risk Officers (CRO) with market-linked compensation.

Recent performance of scheduled commercial banks and soundness (courseware, 2020-21 and H1:2021-22): during 2020-21 scheduled commercial banks (SCBs) reported a discernible improvement in asset quality, capital buffers and profitability, notwithstanding the disruptions of the pandemic; credit offtake remained subdued; deposit growth was highest in seven years, mainly contributed by low-cost current account and savings account (CASA) deposits; credit growth decelerated, reflecting weak demand conditions and risk aversion; the credit-to-GDP ratio increased to a five-year high; investment-deposit ratio rose and credit-deposit ratio declined; the share of PSBs in total advances and in deposits declined since 2010-11 while private sector banks improved; government securities preferred by both PSBs and PVBs. Maturity profile: mismatches in the maturity of assets and liabilities are intrinsic to banking business. International liabilities and assets; off-balance sheet exposure: contingent liabilities declined relative to on-balance sheet exposures. Financial performance: the performance of SCBs in 2020-21 was marked by a discernible increase in profitability as their income remained stable but expenditure declined; net interest margin (NIM) improved; provisions: banks were required to maintain additional provisions of at least 10 per cent on moratorium amounts (Q4:2019-20 and Q1:2020-21). Soundness indicators: capital positions bolstered; the number of banks under the Reserve Bank PCA framework reduced from four at end-March 2020 to one at end-September 2021. Capital adequacy: the capital to risk-weighted assets ratio (CRAR) of SCBs has improved sequentially every quarter from end-March 2020 to reach 16.6 per cent at end-September 2021; the number of banks breaching the regulatory minimum requirement of CRAR (including capital conservation buffer) (10.875 per cent) declined during 2020-21; resource mobilisation by banks through public and rights issues increased sharply; in September 2020 the Parliament approved Rs 20,000 crore capital infusion for PSBs; the leverage ratio (LR), calculated as the ratio of tier-1 capital to total exposure, constrains the build-up of leverage; the Reserve Bank had moderated in October 2019 requiring banks to maintain 4 and 3.5 per cent for domestic systemically important banks and other banks, respectively, as compared with 4.5 per cent earlier. The liquidity coverage ratio (LCR), designed to help banks withstand liquidity pressures in the short-term, requires banks to maintain high quality liquid assets (HQLAs) to meet 30 days net outgo under stressed conditions; the LCR requirement for SCBs was brought down from 100 per cent to 80 per cent in April 2020 and was gradually restored in two phases by April 1, 2021; banks continued to maintain LCR above 100 per cent. Non-performing assets: the moderation in GNPA ratios of banks that began in 2019-20 continued; the GNPA ratio moderated to 7.3 per cent at end-March 2021 and 6.9 per cent at end-September 2021; improvement driven by lower slippages and write-offs; the Restructured Standard Advances (RSA) ratio increased from 0.4 per cent at end-March 2020 to 0.8 per cent at end-March 2021 and 1.8 per cent at end-September 2021; the share of large sized borrower accounts in total advances declined. Recoveries: recovery channels, notably Lok Adalats, witnessed a sizeable decline; initiation of fresh insolvency proceedings under the IBC was suspended for a year till March 2021; asset reconstruction companies (ARCs): the share of SRs subscribed to by banks decreased over the years; the Reserve Bank has been disincentivising banks from holding SRs in excess of 10 per cent of the transaction value of the sale; Frauds: reported fraud cases and amounts; Enforcement actions: the Enforcement Department was created in 2017; monetary penalties on non-compliance. Priority sector credit: PSL accelerated in 2020-21; all bank groups managed to achieve the overall PSL targets; PSL certificates; the revised PSL guidelines of September 2020. Ownership: government ownership; the amalgamation of ten PSBs into four effective April 1, 2020; the share of PSBs in advances; Lakshmi Vilas Bank amalgamated with DBS Bank India Limited from 27 November 2020; as at end-March 2021 21 PVBs. Corporate governance (the discussion paper on Governance in Commercial Banks in India, June 2020; interim set of instructions on April 26, 2021): independent directors, the Audit Committee of the Board (ACB), Risk Management Committee of the Board (RMCB) and Nomination and Remuneration Committee (NRC); executive compensation: revised guidelines on compensation of CEOs / Whole Time Directors (WTDs) / Material Risk Takers (MRTs): the variable pay component should be in the range of 50 to 75 per cent of total pay, a minimum of 60 per cent of variable pay under deferral arrangements; the cash component of variable pay capped between 33 to 50 per cent. Payment systems: total payments declined in value; digital payments grew; RTGS dominates the value; UPI the volume; NEFT and RTGS available 24x7x365 from December 2019 and December 2020; the Payment Infrastructure Development Fund (PIDF) operationalised in January 2021; Reserve Bank Digital Payments Index (DPI) launched January 2021 (five broad parameters with weights: payment enablers 25, payment infrastructure demand-side 10, supply-side 15, payment performance 45, consumer centricity 5 per cent); ATMs: white label ATMs concentrated in rural and semi-urban; consumer protection: Reserve Bank Integrated Ombudsman Scheme (RB-IOS) launched on November 11, 2021; deposit insurance: the DICGC extends deposit insurance to all commercial banks (LABs, PBs, SFBs, RRBs, co-operative banks); insurance cover Rs 5 lakh. Financial inclusion: Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana, Financial Inclusion Plans, business correspondents, microfinance (SHG-BLP), TReDS, regional banking penetration. RBI pandemic response (Section 14.11): the policy repo rate reduced by an unprecedented 115 bps in two phases and cumulatively by 250 bps since February 2019, the CRR reduced by one percentage point (releasing Rs 1,37,000 crore), the MSF window expanded, LTROs and TLTROs, SLF-MF and refinance facilities to AIFIs; regulatory forbearances.

payload.title: Development and supervision of commercial banks: 1950 to 1991
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Initial years (1950-1969):** many banks failed before 1950; the Reserve Bank's inspection powers began in **1940**, widened by the **Banking Companies (Inspection) Ordinance, 1946** (no prior consent of the bank needed); under the **Banking Regulation Act, 1949** the Reserve Bank grants a **licence** only once it is satisfied that the company can **pay depositors in full**. Inspection shifted from a **check on the amount of paid-up capital and reserves** to a **judgement on the quality of a bank's financial position, management and methods**; **regular, systematic inspection of every bank began in March 1950**. The **Act was amended in January 1957** (including **refinance** provisions). After the **Palai Central Bank and Laxmi Commercial Bank** collapse (**1960**), the Reserve Bank gained powers for **amalgamation** and **speedy de-licensing**, strengthened inspection (**1961**), looked at **capital adequacy norms** and began **deposit insurance**. The 1960-68 thrust: **soundness**, **consolidation**, **protection of small depositors** (compulsory amalgamations and liquidations), **correcting lopsided branch distribution** by **branch licensing**, and **social control (1967)** over credit deployment.

**Nationalisation and consolidation (1969-91):** **14 banks nationalised on 19 July 1969**; boards constituted on **18 July 1970**; the **National Credit Council** and the **Lead Bank Scheme (December 1969)**; a **branch expansion plan for 1972-74**; **Annual Appraisal** inspection added in **1977-78**; **6 more banks nationalised in 1980**; the target of **40 per cent priority sector advances by 1985**; the **Annual Financial Review from January 1985**; a **Working Group on inspection (December 1981)**.

**1990s reforms:** efficiency and profitability had fallen (directed credit, over-staffing, weak technology), so the **Narasimham Committee (1991)** led to **interest rate deregulation**, **lower CRR and SLR**, **operational autonomy** and prudential norms; **guidelines for entry of private banks in 1993**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Supervision moved from checking solvency to appraising management and operations.

self_check.prompt_text: When was the policy of systematic periodical inspections of all banks announced?

payload.title: Prudential indicators, supervisory returns and risk management in banks
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Supervisory tools:** the Reserve Bank follows **Basel principles**: **capital adequacy**, **asset classification**, **income recognition**, **market valuation of assets** and **recovery of NPAs**, using **on-site** and **off-site** supervision. **Micro-prudential indicators** by **CAMELS** category (**capital ratio; sectoral concentration, foreign currency lending, NPAs, connected lending; expense ratios; ROA and ROE; loan-to-deposit ratio and inter-bank rate spreads; risk management and audit systems; foreign exchange, interest rate, equity and commodity price sensitivity; market-based indicators**) aggregate into the **AMPI**; they are combined with **macroeconomic indicators** and **stress tests** to form **macro-prudential indicators**.

**Returns:** **1999 ALM guidelines** introduced the **Statement of Structural Liquidity** (fortnightly: **domestic, foreign, combined Indian operations, overseas, consolidated**) and **interest rate sensitivity** (earnings perspective by **Traditional Gap Analysis, TGA**). **November 2012** revisions aligned with **Basel III**: **Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR)** and **Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR)** returns (**BLR 1 to 5**), and **Duration Gap Analysis (DGA)** (modified duration gap, by currency, monthly) **in addition to** TGA.

**Risk management (October 1999 guidelines):** **four risks** (**market, credit, legal, operational**) plus **systemic risk**; the **Board** sets risk parameters; implementation by a **Risk Management Committee**; a high-level **Credit Policy Committee (CPC)** and a separate, independent **department for credit risk management**; the **ALCO** and CPC integrate credit and market risk. **Credit risk** tools: Board-approved **loan policy**, **delegation of powers**, exposure limits (**single borrower, group, industry, region, sector**), **rating systems**, **loan review mechanism** and **rigorous evaluation of off-balance sheet and inter-bank/country exposures**. **Market risk** tools: **duration, EaR, VaR, simulation, RAROC**. **Interest rate risk:** **gap limits**, **VaR/duration/simulation** and **stress tests**; **currency risk**: **gap limits** with RBI approval and **VaR on forwards**; **operational risk**: proper **measurement and control systems**.

**Regulatory approaches to market risk:** **building block (BBA, as in the 1988 Basel market risk standards)**, **internal models (IMA)** and **pre-commitment (PCA)**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Banks control risk through board policy, limits, committees and independent measurement.

self_check.prompt_text: What additional return and what analysis were introduced for interest rate risk by the revised 2012 guidelines?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Duration gap analysis (and LCR/NSFR returns for liquidity), alongside the traditional gap analysis.

payload.title: Regulatory policies and supervision of scheduled commercial banks (2020-22), the PCA framework and PSB mergers
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Covid-19 relief (temporary):** **Resolution Framework (6 August 2020)** to restructure **eligible corporate and personal loans without an ownership change and without downgrading to NPA** (borrowers **standard and not over 30 days past due on 1 March 2020**; invoked by **31 December 2020**; implemented within **90 days (personal)** or **180 days (others)**), guided by the **Kamath Committee**'s **five financial parameters and sector thresholds**; **Resolution Framework 2.0 (5 May 2021)** for **individuals and small businesses** (**aggregate exposure up to Rs 50 crore**). **Ex-gratia** payment of the **difference between compound and simple interest** on loans **up to Rs 2 crore** for the **moratorium period (1 March to 31 August 2020)**. **Gold loans for non-agricultural uses: LTV raised from 75 to 90 per cent**. **Dividend** not to be paid from **2019-20 profits**. **CRR cut to 3 per cent (28 March 2020)** and **restored to 3.5 and 4 per cent** in 2021; **CRR exemption** for **new MSME credit up to Rs 25 lakh per borrower**; **HTM ceiling raised to 22 per cent** (till **31 March 2023**, **restored to 19.5 per cent in stages**); **MSF** dip into SLR **raised to 3 per cent of NDTL** (normal **2 per cent** restored from **1 January 2022**); **last 0.625 per cent of the CCB** and the **NSFR** deferred to **1 October 2021**; the **regulatory retail portfolio limit raised from Rs 5 crore to Rs 7.5 crore** (risk weight **75 per cent**); **LTV-linked risk weights** for **new housing loans (16 October 2020 to 31 March 2022)**; rules on **opening current accounts and CC/OD** tightened from **August 2021**.

**Supervision:** the **Board for Financial Supervision (November 1994)** supervises **SCBs, AIFIs, co-operative banks and NBFCs**; **April 2021 guidelines on appointing statutory auditors** (**independence, conflict of interest**, first extended to **UCBs and NBFCs**).

**Revised Prompt Corrective Action framework (from 1 January 2022):** **timely supervisory intervention** and **market discipline**; key areas **capital (CRAR/CET1), asset quality (net NPA) and leverage (Tier I leverage ratio)**; **negative ROA is no longer a trigger**; PCA is generally based on **audited annual results and supervisory assessment** and applies to **foreign banks' branches and subsidiaries**; **exit** requires **no breach for four continuous quarters (including an audited annual statement)** plus **supervisory comfort**; **mandatory actions**: **restrictions on dividends/remittance of profits and on branch expansion**, **promoter or parent to bring capital**, and **limits on capital expenditure** other than technology. **Lakshmi Vilas Bank** (under PCA) merged with **DBS Bank on 27 November 2020**; **IDBI Bank, UCO Bank and Indian Overseas Bank** exited (2021); only **Central Bank of India** remained under PCA.

**PSB mergers (1 April 2020):** **ten banks into four**: **PNB** (Oriental Bank of Commerce, United Bank of India), **Canara Bank** (Syndicate Bank), **Union Bank of India** (Corporation Bank, Andhra Bank), **Indian Bank** (Allahabad Bank); customers became customers of the **anchor bank**; benefits: **bigger capital base**, **scale**, **efficiency**, **larger customer base**, **global competitiveness**; banks were to appoint **specialised Chief Risk Officers**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Regulatory relief during the pandemic was temporary, while PCA and mergers address structural weakness.

self_check.prompt_text: Under the revised PCA framework, which indicators are monitored for scheduled commercial banks?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Capital (CRAR and CET1), asset quality (net NPA ratio) and leverage (Tier I leverage ratio).

payload.title: Recent performance, soundness indicators and developments in the banking sector (2020-22)
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Overall (2020-21):** better **asset quality, capital buffers and profitability** despite the pandemic; **credit offtake weak**, **deposit growth strongest in seven years** (led by **CASA**); **credit-deposit ratio down**, **investment-deposit ratio up**; **government securities** preferred; **PSB share in advances and deposits falling since 2010-11**.

**Soundness:** **CRAR rose every quarter to 16.6 per cent (September 2021)**; banks breaching the **10.875 per cent** minimum (including the CCB) fell; **leverage ratio** minimums **4 per cent (D-SIBs) and 3.5 per cent (others)** (earlier **4.5**); **LCR** (30 day stressed outflows covered by **HQLAs**) requirement was **cut from 100 to 80 per cent in April 2020** and restored by **1 April 2021** while banks held **above 100 per cent**; **GNPA ratio 7.3 per cent (March 2021) and 6.9 per cent (September 2021)** via **lower slippages and write-offs**; **Restructured Standard Advances rose** (0.4 to 1.8 per cent); the number of banks under **PCA fell from four to one**.

**Recoveries and ARCs:** recoveries through **Lok Adalats** fell; **fresh IBC proceedings were suspended for a year to March 2021**; the Reserve Bank **disincentivised banks from holding security receipts above 10 per cent of the sale value**.

**Other themes:** **priority sector lending** met targets; **ownership** (PSB mergers, **Lakshmi Vilas Bank into DBS**, **21 PVBs**); **corporate governance** (**Audit, Risk Management and Nomination and Remuneration committees**; **executive pay: variable pay 50-75 per cent of total, at least 60 per cent of it deferred, cash part 33-50 per cent**); **payments** (**RTGS and NEFT 24x7**, **UPI** leads in volume, **Payment Infrastructure Development Fund (January 2021)**, **Digital Payments Index** with **five parameters**); **consumer protection** (**RB-Integrated Ombudsman Scheme, 11 November 2021**; **DICGC cover Rs 5 lakh**); **financial inclusion** (**PMJDY, business correspondents, SHG-BLP, TReDS**).
